teaser: A woody spiral opens in dry air and closes when wet.
title: Pinecones
question: Why would a tree open its cones only when the air is dry?
idea: Many common pinecones open when dry and close when wet. Water changes the shape of their woody scales, helping time the release of seeds.

curiosity.intro: Bring a fallen cone to the porch table and follow a slow change.
curiosity.carryForward: Keep two small drawings: open and closed.

questions.question: What is a pinecone made of?
questions.notice: Follow a spiral around the cone.
questions.say: A pinecone is a woody seed case with many overlapping parts called scales. Seeds grow tucked beside the scales. The scales wind around the cone in spirals.
questions.try: Count the scales you can see on one side, then draw one spiral.

questions.question: Why are there gaps in a dry cone?
questions.say: When many common pinecones dry, their scales bend outward. The open spaces let ripe seeds leave. A light wing helps many pine seeds catch the breeze.
questions.try: Set a dry cone on a dish and sketch its outline. Leave room beside your drawing for a second shape.

questions.question: What changes when a cone gets wet?
questions.notice: Compare the close scales with your open-cone drawing.
questions.say: Wet or humid conditions add water to the scales. Parts of each scale take in water differently, so the woody tissue bends inward. The cone closes. A fallen cone can still do this without muscles.
questions.try: Use two fallen cones or cones from a craft bin. Put one in a dry dish and briefly wet the other in a shallow dish of water. With Big beside you, check their scales over time and draw both shapes. Collect fallen brown cones with Big nearby; leave green cones on branches, keep feet on the ground, and wash hands afterward.

questions.question: Why wait for dry air?
questions.notice: Find the thin wing beside a seed.
questions.say: Winged seeds can drift on a dry breeze. When wet, they can cling to a scale instead. Closing in damp weather helps keep seeds inside until conditions are better for leaving. Different kinds of pinecones do not all open in exactly the same way.
questions.try: Let the damp cone dry on an empty dish. Check it later. What do you think the scales will do?

reading.title: The cone that changed its shape

reading.parentNote: Ages 6-8. Welcome spoken answers and dictation. Connect pinecone, scale, moisture, humid, tissue, and seed to the scenes.

beats.title: A woody spiral
beats.passage: Little Wonderer set a fallen pinecone on the porch table. It felt woody, but it was not a piece of bark. “A pinecone is a seed case,” said Big Wonderer. Its many parts are called scales. They overlap in a spiral, winding around the cone. Little followed the spiral with a curious gaze.

foldable.heading: A woody spiral
foldable.body: Little found a woody seed case. Its scales overlapped in a spiral. Big called it a pinecone. What was hiding inside?

beats.title: Room between scales
beats.passage: The dry cone had gaps between its scales. Dry means there is little moisture, or water, around it. The scales spread outward like small shelves. Seeds could slip through the spaces. Little drew the wide shape. Would the cone stay open if the air changed?
beats.prompt: How could a seed leave the dry cone?

foldable.heading: Room for seeds
foldable.body: The dry cone had gaps between its scales. Seeds could slip through those spaces. Little drew its wide, open shape.

beats.title: A cone closes
beats.passage: Big placed another cone in a shallow dish of water. Over time, its scales curled closer together. Wet scales take in a little water and bend inward. Humid air has water in it too. Little checked the drawing again. The cone had become narrower without anyone squeezing it.
beats.prompt: What changed as the cone became wet?

foldable.heading: A slow closing
foldable.body: The wet cone took in a little water. Its scales bent inward and closed the gaps. Little watched its shape grow narrow.

beats.title: Two dishes, one clue
beats.passage: One dish stayed dry. The other held the damp cone. Little sketched both shapes in a notebook: open and closed. “Let’s give the damp one time to dry,” said Big. They left it on a dry dish. Later, spaces began to appear between its scales again.
beats.prompt: What would make the two-dish test a fair comparison?

foldable.heading: Two dishes, one clue
foldable.body: Little drew the open cone and the closed cone. When the damp cone dried, spaces began to appear between its scales again.

beats.title: Water bends the scales
beats.passage: Little leaned toward the magnifier. A scale was made of plant tissue, the material that makes up plant parts. Different parts of that tissue take in water differently. That makes the scale bend. The fallen cone needed no muscles to move. Water in, water out: its shape could change.
beats.prompt: What makes a scale bend without muscles?

foldable.heading: Water makes it bend
foldable.body: Parts of a scale take in water differently. This bends the plant tissue. The fallen cone can move without muscles.

beats.title: A day for seeds
beats.passage: A winged seed rested beside the open cone. Its thin wing could catch a breeze. Wet seeds can cling instead of drifting. “Why would a tree open its cones only when the air is dry?” Little wondered. Their two drawings held a clue.
beats.prompt: Why might dry weather help a winged seed travel?

foldable.heading: A day for seeds
foldable.body: A seed with a thin wing lay beside the open cone. Could dry air help it travel? Little kept the question in the notebook.

math.title: Compare cones, round counts
math.intro: Compare two counts or round one count to the nearest ten.

tasks.prompt: Little counts 47 open cones and 74 closed cones on two trays. Fill the circle with >, <, or =. Which count is greater?
tasks.hint: Compare the tens first: 4 tens and 7 tens.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Big records 32 visible scales. What is this count rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Find 32 between 30 and 40. Which ten is closer?
tasks.worked: 32 rounds to 30 because it is 2 away from 30 and 8 away from 40.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: One notebook shows 68 dry cones; another shows 59 damp cones. Fill the circle with >, <, or =. Which count is greater?
tasks.hint: Compare 6 tens with 5 tens before looking at the ones.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Little draws 85 moisture marks beside the cone pictures. What is the count rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: 85 is halfway between 80 and 90. Halfway rounds up.
tasks.worked: 85 rounds to 90. A ones digit of 5 rounds up to the next ten.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Big and Little each count 26 scales on one side of a cone. Fill the circle with >, <, or =. What is the shared count?
tasks.hint: Compare the tens and the ones. Both counts match.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: A page shows 56 open scales. What is the count rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Find 56 between 50 and 60. It is past the halfway point.
tasks.worked: 56 rounds to 60 because it is 4 away from 60 and 6 away from 50.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose a rounding task and show its two nearby tens on a number line.
math.printNote: Show your thinking with numbers, marks, or words.
math.parentNote: Ages 6-8 math. Compare two-digit counts and round to the nearest ten. A ones digit of 5 rounds up. Counts describe story collections, not a fixed number of scales on each cone.
math.answerKeyIntro: Ages 6-8 math. Compare tens, then ones. For rounding, locate the two nearby tens and find the closer one; halfway rounds up.

writing.title: A small change, in words
writing.intro: Give a clear command for watching a cone.
writing.draw: Draw an open cone beside a closed cone. Show the gaps between the scales.
writing.check: Does your command begin with an action word, such as Watch, Compare, or Draw?
writing.parentNote: Welcome speech, dictation, invented spelling, or writing. One command is enough. Example: “Watch one dry cone and one damp cone, then draw how the scales look.”

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: A dry cone usually has open scales with gaps. A wet cone usually has close scales and a narrower shape.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Different parts of a scale take in water differently. The plant tissue bends as it gains or loses water; it does not need muscles.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: In dry conditions, scales open and winged seeds can drift on a breeze. Wet seeds can cling to the scales.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a command spoken, dictated, drawn, or written. Example: “Watch one dry cone and one damp cone, then draw how the scales look.”

parentGuidance: Ages 6-8. Collect fallen brown cones with Big nearby; leave green cones on branches, keep feet on the ground, and wash hands afterward. Use shallow dishes, with a grown-up nearby. Changes may take hours; revisit later without a timer or deadline. Many mature common pinecones open dry and close wet, but species differ, and some cones need special conditions to first open. Mature scale tissue is no longer living; its structure still swells unevenly with moisture and bends. The cone is not choosing or using muscles. Empty fallen cones can still change shape. The diorama shows this moisture response faster than it happens at the table, with a qualitative view inside the cone rather than a measured scale angle.

questions.prompt: What are the woody parts stacked around a pinecone called?
questions.answer: They are scales, arranged in spirals around the cone.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to a common pinecone as it dries?
questions.answer: As the cone dries, its scales open wider, making space for seeds to leave.

questions.prompt: What makes a wet pinecone’s scales close?
choices: Water makes parts of the scale swell differently
questions.answer: Water makes parts of the scale swell differently, bending the woody tissue inward.

questions.prompt: Why can dry weather be a good time for winged seeds to leave?
choices: A dry winged seed can drift on a breeze
Seeds need to stay wet to drift
questions.answer: A dry winged seed can drift on a breeze. Wet seeds can cling to the cone instead.

why: Comparing wet and dry pinecones helps your child connect a change in shape to water and seed release.
